executiveSummary.oneLiner: AlgoForge turns source code into plain explanations and step-by-step visualizations, so you can see what your code is doing instead of guessing.
executiveSummary.problemStatement: Reading code is one thing. Seeing how it runs, one step at a time, is much harder. Most learners are left imagining what happens inside a loop or a recursive call.
executiveSummary.solutionOverview: AlgoForge keeps three jobs apart: analysing the code, generating visualization JSON, and drawing it on screen. The AI explains the code, ForgeCode turns that analysis into JSON, and the visualizer plays it back frame by frame. You can also ask follow-up questions about your own code.
primaryUsers: Anyone studying algorithms and data structures
keyCapabilities: AI source code analysis with structured explanations
Frame-by-frame algorithm visualization with real-time state changes
Optimization suggestions and doubt solving
LangChain pipelines that return schema-compliant JSON

Workspace drafts and explanation sessions

AI provider availability and usage limits affect generation
ForgeCode output quality depends on the input context and instructions

executiveSummary.oneLiner: Hermes is a real-time chat app with end-to-end encrypted private chats and group chat, running on a k3s Kubernetes cluster on GCP that I built and automated myself.
executiveSummary.problemStatement: I wanted to build a chat system and solve the whole stack on my own: real-time messaging, private-by-design encryption, sign-in, cloud infrastructure, containers, delivery pipelines and monitoring, all without managed services doing the hard parts for me.
executiveSummary.solutionOverview: A Spring Boot backend serves REST APIs for sign-in and data, and WebSocket/STOMP for live messaging. Private messages are encrypted in the browser with the WebCrypto API, so the server only ever stores ciphertext. Terraform and Ansible set up the GCP infrastructure, k3s runs the app, and a GitHub Actions pipeline with Trivy scanning is ready to deploy it.
primaryUsers: People who want private, real-time chat
keyCapabilities: End-to-end encrypted private chats: ECDH P-256 key exchange and AES-GCM per message via WebCrypto
Real-time private and group messaging over WebSocket/STOMP
Google OAuth2 and email/password sign-in with OTP verification and password reset
JWT access and refresh tokens in secure cookies
Secure image sharing with Redis caching
Live presence and typing indicators
Per-user sliding-window rate limiting in Redis
Group creation, membership and group chat
Kubernetes setup: Deployments, StatefulSets, HPA, NetworkPolicies, CronJob and cert-manager
CI/CD pipeline with Trivy scanning and smoke testing (written, not yet switched on)
Prometheus and Grafana monitoring
knownLimitations: Group messages are not end-to-end encrypted
The in-memory STOMP broker does not scale horizontally. RabbitMQ is on the roadmap
Local file storage does not survive pod restarts
Message history is limited to the last 24 hours

Real user traffic and load testing

architecture.architectureRationale: WebSocket/STOMP keeps chat fast, while REST handles sign-in and data. Encrypting in the browser means even a compromised server can't read private messages. Terraform, Ansible and k3s give a repeatable setup with no managed-service lock-in. The in-memory STOMP broker is the known scaling bottleneck, and RabbitMQ is the planned fix.

executiveSummary.oneLiner: Pokeverse is a real-time multiplayer game platform that provides the shared basics (sign-in, rooms, live events, chat and state), so each new game can plug in without rebuilding them.
executiveSummary.problemStatement: Every multiplayer game needs the same things: players who can sign in, rooms they can join, live events, chat and saved state. Rebuilding them for every game is wasteful and leads to uneven quality. Pokeverse puts them in one reusable platform.
executiveSummary.solutionOverview: A Spring Boot backend offers shared services for sign-in, rooms, live messaging over WebSocket/STOMP and storage. Games plug in as modules and use those services. The Pokémon Quiz shows it off with single-player and multiplayer modes, room-scoped broadcasting and live scoring. PostgreSQL keeps the history; Redis holds the fast-changing game state.
primaryUsers: Hosts who create and run rooms
Admins who manage game content (RBAC on the roadmap)
keyCapabilities: OAuth2 sign-in with JWT access and refresh tokens
Reusable room creation, join/leave and session handling
Live events over WebSocket/STOMP, topic-based and queue-based
Shared in-room chat that is saved
Event-driven game engine that coordinates player actions, scoring and round progression
Pluggable game modules, with platform concerns kept separate from game rules
Two data stores: PostgreSQL 17 (Flyway-managed) for durable data, Redis 7 for fast live state
Pokémon Quiz: single-player with session tracking and analysis, and room-based multiplayer
knownLimitations: Role-based access control (RBAC) is not built yet; admin access currently uses request parameters
Only one game module (Pokémon Quiz) exists so far
No Kubernetes deployment yet; Docker Compose is used for local development

card.tagline: A scientific calculator with no eval(), on purpose.
card.summary: A scientific expression evaluator built from scratch with classic compiler ideas. It answers one curious question: what really happens between typing an expression and seeing a number?
bullets: Tokenizer, implicit multiplication, Shunting-Yard and a stack evaluator
50+ functions and 70+ operators with domain checks
100+ test cases and no external math libraries
Explained in a public Medium article

executiveSummary.oneLiner: A scientific expression evaluator built from scratch: tokenising, adding hidden multiplication signs, converting to postfix with Shunting-Yard, then evaluating with a stack. It has 50+ functions, 70+ operators and no external math libraries.
executiveSummary.problemStatement: Most calculator projects just call eval() or a library. This one asks how calculators and parsers actually work: what happens between typing '2 + 3 * sin(pi/4)^2' and a number appearing?
executiveSummary.solutionOverview: A Python package exposes a StackQueueCalculator. It tokenises the input, injects implicit multiplication, converts to postfix with Shunting-Yard, and evaluates the result using a function registry covering arithmetic, trig, hyperbolic, logs, combinatorics and constants. A Medium article explains the algorithm and the choices behind it.
primaryUsers: Developers and learners curious about parsing and DSA
Students studying compiler techniques and stack-based evaluation
Developers who want a programmable scientific calculator
keyCapabilities: Tokenisation with implicit multiplication ('2pi' becomes '2 * pi')
Shunting-Yard conversion from infix to postfix with full precedence and associativity
Stack-based postfix (RPN) evaluation
50+ functions: arithmetic, trig, hyperbolic, logarithms, combinatorics (nPr, nCr, GCD, LCM) and utilities (abs, floor, ceil, hypot, atan2)
5 constants (π, e, τ, φ, ans), memory operations (M+, M-, MR, MC) and last-answer reference
Domain checks (no sqrt of a negative, no division by zero) and overflow protection
100+ test cases across 9 categories
No external math dependencies
knownLimitations: No CLI or GUI; it is used through the Python API
History and memory are not saved between runs
The random function ignores its argument
No complex numbers, so sqrt(-1) is rejected

shortTerm: Show evaluate_with_steps() in the usage docs for learning
midTerm: Add a simple TUI or GUI
longTerm: Add a plugin system for custom functions

architecture.overview: A single-process Python library where an expression flows through a straight pipeline: tokeniser, implicit multiplication injector, postfix converter, stack evaluator. Math functions are grouped by domain (trig, hyperbolic, math) in a registry. StackQueueCalculator runs the pipeline and keeps memory and the last answer.

graph TB

A[User Expression]
B[Tokenizer]

D[Postfix Converter - Shunting-Yard]

components.name: StackQueueCalculator
responsibilities: Run tokenisation, postfix conversion and stack evaluation
Keep memory and the last answer
Register functions and constants in the function registry

components.name: Tokenizer
responsibilities: Turn the input string into typed tokens (numbers, operators, functions, constants)
Tell unary negation apart from binary subtraction
Spot named constants and function calls

components.name: Implicit Multiplication Injector
responsibilities: Insert missing * tokens without causing ambiguity ('2pi' becomes '2 * pi', '2(3+4)' becomes '2 * (3+4)')

components.name: Postfix Converter
responsibilities: Use Shunting-Yard to turn infix into RPN
Handle parentheses, unary functions and binary functions

components.name: Postfix Evaluator
responsibilities: Evaluate the postfix expression with an operand stack
Call the function registry for named unary and binary functions
Check domains and guard against overflow

components.name: Function Modules
responsibilities: Provide math, trig and hyperbolic functions
Combinatorics with overflow protection (factorial of large numbers)

steps: Pass an expression string to evaluate()
The tokeniser turns it into typed tokens
The injector adds any missing * operators
The converter applies Shunting-Yard to produce an RPN sequence
The stack evaluator computes the result, checking domains along the way
Call memory add, subtract, recall or clear
The calculator updates its in-process memory
The memory value can be used as an operand in later expressions

architecture.architectureRationale: The tokeniser, Shunting-Yard and postfix pipeline mirrors the front end of a classic compiler, so each stage has one clear job and can be tested alone. With no external math libraries, nothing hides how it works, which is the whole point.

backend.name: Python
backend.purpose: Runtime, standard math utilities and all parsing logic
backend.tradeOffs: Single process with no built-in UI; the GIL limits parallelism, which doesn't matter here

backend.purpose: Optional coloured output in the test runner
backend.tradeOffs: Not needed for the calculator itself; test-only

backend.name: uv
backend.purpose: Fast Python package manager with pyproject.toml packaging and .python-version pinning
backend.tradeOffs: Newer than pip and less universal, but much faster

rejectedAlternatives.reasonRejected: A security risk, and it would skip the whole learning point
The goal is to build the algorithm, not call it
It needs a separate numeric type through the whole pipeline; it's on the long-term roadmap
